GS.what: Advises on mergers, underwrites securities, trades for institutions and manages assets - the purest investment bank at scale.
GS.rev: Global banking and markets roughly 65-70%, asset and wealth management ~30%, platform solutions small. Americas is the majority.
GS.gm: Watch return on tangible equity (mid-to-high teens in good years), compensation ratio and the mix between volatile trading and stable fees.
GS.mgmt: David Solomon is CEO. Partner culture means employee ownership is meaningful by Wall Street standards.
GS.comp: Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, Bank of America, Evercore and the boutiques in advisory.
GS.moat: Relationships, league-table reputation and a risk-management franchise that is hard to build. Talent can walk, which caps the moat.
GS.ind: Capital markets activity is cyclical; the private credit and alternatives push is the structural growth attempt.
GS.risk: A closed IPO and M&A window lasting years, with trading revenue normalising at the same time.
GS.implied: Around two times tangible book implies sustained high returns - the top of Goldmans historical range.
GS.debate: Bulls say a deal recovery plus growing asset management fees re-rate it. Bears say peak book multiple on peak trading revenue is how you lose money in banks.
GS.disprove: Advisory backlog shrinking; trading revenue falling faster than expenses; asset management fee growth stalling; book multiple compressing.

WFC.what: A large US retail and commercial bank - deposits, mortgages, auto lending and commercial banking - recently released from its asset cap.
WFC.rev: Consumer banking and lending ~40%, commercial banking ~20%, corporate and investment banking ~20%, wealth the rest. Essentially all US.
WFC.gm: Watch net interest income, efficiency ratio (around 65%) and ROTCE (low-to-mid teens, with room to improve now the cap is gone).
WFC.mgmt: Charlie Scharf has led the clean-up since 2019. Insider ownership small; regulatory remediation is the defining management task.
WFC.comp: JPMorgan, Bank of America, Citigroup, plus regional banks in commercial lending.
WFC.moat: Branch and deposit scale, and the hardest-to-replicate asset in banking: a cheap, sticky retail deposit base.
WFC.ind: Mature; the company-specific story is balance sheet growth post asset cap.
WFC.risk: A commercial real estate credit cycle, or a return of regulatory problems that reimpose constraints.
WFC.implied: The price implies ROTCE improving toward the mid-teens as the balance sheet grows again.
WFC.debate: Bulls say the asset cap removal unlocks years of growth and buybacks. Bears note office CRE exposure and a long history of control failures.
WFC.disprove: CRE reserve builds rising; expense targets missed; ROTCE not improving; new consent orders.

RTX.what: Sells jet engines (Pratt and Whitney), aerospace components (Collins) and missiles and defence systems (Raytheon) to airlines and governments.
RTX.rev: Collins Aerospace ~35%, Pratt and Whitney ~30%, Raytheon defence ~35%. US government is roughly 40% of sales.
RTX.gm: Segment margins run in the low-to-mid teens. Like GE, original equipment is sold thin and the money is in aftermarket parts and service.
RTX.mgmt: Chris Calio is CEO. Insider ownership small; the GTF engine recall was the defining recent challenge.
RTX.comp: GE Aerospace and Safran in engines, Lockheed Martin and Northrop in defence, Honeywell in components.
RTX.moat: Certified installed base, decades-long defence programme positions, and aftermarket annuities. Programme wins lock in twenty years of revenue.
RTX.ind: Both halves growing: air traffic recovery and elevated global defence budgets.
RTX.risk: Another powder-metal style engine quality issue, or defence budget reallocation away from its programmes.
RTX.implied: A mid-20s P/E implies the GTF problems are behind it and defence backlog converts smoothly.
RTX.debate: Bulls say a record backlog across both aerospace and defence with margin recovery ahead. Bears remember how expensive the engine recall was.
RTX.disprove: Further GTF charges; defence segment margin not recovering; backlog conversion slowing; free cash flow missing guidance.

CRWD.what: Sells cloud-native endpoint and cloud security software on the Falcon platform, by subscription, to enterprises.
CRWD.rev: Subscription revenue is over 95%. Modules beyond endpoint - cloud, identity, SIEM - are the growth driver. US around two-thirds.
CRWD.gm: Subscription gross margin around 78-80%. Single lightweight agent, one cloud platform; the marginal customer is cheap to serve.
CRWD.mgmt: Co-founder George Kurtz is CEO. Founder-led with meaningful ownership; the July 2024 outage was the key test of the brand.
CRWD.comp: Palo Alto Networks, SentinelOne, Microsoft Defender, Zscaler in adjacent segments.
CRWD.moat: Data network effects across trillions of daily events, single-agent architecture that makes adding modules nearly free, and high switching costs once the agent is deployed fleet-wide.
CRWD.ind: Endpoint and cloud security budgets growing faster than IT; SIEM is the newest land grab.
CRWD.risk: Another global outage destroying the trust that the entire pitch rests on, or Microsoft bundling Defender at zero marginal price.
CRWD.implied: At well over 20 times sales and a very high multiple of free cash flow, the price implies 20%+ growth persisting for many years with module attach continuing.
CRWD.debate: Bulls say it is the consolidation winner with best-in-class retention. Bears say the multiple leaves no room for a single stumble.
CRWD.disprove: Net new ARR growth slowing; net retention below 110%; module adoption rates plateauing; customer commitment packages masking discounting.

TXN.what: Sells analog and embedded processing chips - tens of thousands of simple, long-lived parts - to industrial, auto and electronics makers.
TXN.rev: Analog ~75%, embedded processing ~20%. Industrial and automotive together are roughly two-thirds of revenue. Direct sales through its own channel.
TXN.gm: Gross margin around 57-60%, down from 65%+ as new 300mm fabs depreciate. TI owns its fabs, which is a cost advantage at high utilisation and a burden at low.
TXN.mgmt: Haviv Ilan is CEO. Insider ownership small; TI has an unusually explicit free-cash-flow-per-share philosophy.
TXN.comp: Analog Devices, Infineon, STMicroelectronics, NXP, Microchip.
TXN.moat: A catalogue of 80,000 parts designed into products for a decade or more, 300mm analog manufacturing cost advantage, and direct customer relationships.
TXN.ind: Industrial and auto semiconductors have been in a prolonged downturn; content per vehicle keeps rising long-term.
TXN.risk: The capex cycle finishing just as demand stays weak, so depreciation lands on soft revenue and free cash flow per share stalls for years.
TXN.implied: A P/E in the 30s on trough earnings implies a full cyclical recovery plus the capex programme paying off.
TXN.debate: Bulls say the 300mm investment creates a decade of cost advantage. Bears say management spent through the downturn and free cash flow per share has gone nowhere.
TXN.disprove: Industrial and auto revenue not recovering; gross margin staying below 58%; capex not falling as promised; free cash flow per share flat again.

ANET.what: Sells high-speed data centre switches and the EOS network operating system to cloud providers and large enterprises.
ANET.rev: Product roughly 80%, services and software support ~20%. Customer concentration is high - Microsoft and Meta have each been over 10%.
ANET.gm: Gross margin around 62-65%, unusually high for hardware, because the value is in the software and the merchant silicon keeps cost down.
ANET.mgmt: Jayshree Ullal has been CEO since 2008; Andy Bechtolsheim is chief architect and a major shareholder. Genuine founder-level alignment.
ANET.comp: Cisco, NVIDIA (Spectrum and InfiniBand), white-box vendors with SONiC.
ANET.moat: A single software image across the portfolio that network engineers trust, plus deep co-design with the largest cloud buyers.
ANET.ind: AI back-end networking is one of the fastest-growing pockets in infrastructure.
ANET.risk: Losing a top customer to NVIDIA Spectrum or to in-house designs - two customers are a large share of revenue.
ANET.implied: A multiple in the 40s implies AI networking share gains continue and margins stay at record levels.
ANET.debate: Bulls say Ethernet wins the AI back end and Arista is the default. Bears point at concentration risk and NVIDIA competing directly.
ANET.disprove: A named large customer shifting to Spectrum; gross margin falling below 60%; deferred revenue growth slowing; cloud titan spend guidance cut.

IBM.what: Sells hybrid cloud software (Red Hat), consulting and mainframe systems to large enterprises and governments.
IBM.rev: Software ~45%, consulting ~33%, infrastructure ~20%. Mainframe cycles still move the numbers. Americas around half.
IBM.gm: Gross margin around 57-59%, rising as software mix grows and consulting is managed for margin rather than growth.
IBM.mgmt: Arvind Krishna is CEO and bet the company on Red Hat and hybrid cloud. Insider ownership minimal; dividend is a priority.
IBM.comp: Accenture in consulting, Microsoft and VMware in hybrid infrastructure, AWS and Azure in cloud.
IBM.moat: Mainframe lock-in that has lasted fifty years, Red Hat Linux as an enterprise standard, and government and bank relationships.
IBM.ind: Legacy IT is flat; the hybrid cloud and AI consulting pockets are growing.
IBM.risk: Consulting demand weakening while software growth is too small to carry the company - the historical IBM pattern.
IBM.implied: A high-20s P/E implies sustained mid single-digit revenue growth, which IBM has rarely achieved.
IBM.debate: Bulls point to a genuine software transformation and AI book of business. Bears say the revenue base has been flat for a decade and buybacks did the rest.
IBM.disprove: Software growth below 8%; consulting bookings declining; free cash flow guidance missed; mainframe cycle rolling over.

GEV.what: Sells power generation equipment - gas turbines, wind turbines and grid electrification systems - to utilities and data centre developers.
GEV.rev: Power (gas turbines and services) ~50%, electrification ~25% and fastest growing, wind ~25% and loss-making. Global utility customers.
GEV.gm: Margins vary sharply: gas power and electrification are profitable and improving; offshore wind has destroyed value with contract losses.
GEV.mgmt: Scott Strazik is CEO of the 2024 spin-off from GE. Insider ownership small; the equity story is margin expansion.
GEV.comp: Siemens Energy and Mitsubishi in gas turbines, Vestas in wind, Schneider, ABB and Hitachi in grid.
GEV.moat: Gas turbine installed base with multi-decade service contracts, plus a grid equipment backlog nobody can fill quickly - capacity is sold out for years.
GEV.ind: Electricity demand is growing for the first time in twenty years, driven by data centres and electrification.
GEV.risk: A data centre power build-out pause, or further offshore wind contract losses eating the profits of the other segments.
GEV.implied: A P/E near 50 implies the power and electrification backlog converts at much higher margins for many years.
GEV.debate: Bulls say it is the purest way to own electricity demand growth. Bears say wind still loses money and the multiple assumes flawless execution.
GEV.disprove: Gas turbine slot reservations not converting to firm orders; wind charges recurring; electrification margin not expanding; utility capex guidance cut.

C.what: A global bank focused on corporate treasury services, markets, and a US consumer card business, in the middle of a long restructuring.
C.rev: Services (treasury and securities) ~25% and the crown jewel, markets ~25%, banking ~15%, US personal banking ~30%. Genuinely global.
C.gm: Watch ROTCE (still below peers at high single to low double digits), efficiency ratio and CET1 capital.
C.mgmt: Jane Fraser is CEO and is simplifying a bank that had become unmanageable. Insider ownership small.
C.comp: JPMorgan, Bank of America, HSBC and Standard Chartered in global transaction banking.
C.moat: The global treasury and custody network is genuinely hard to replicate - it clears in nearly every currency. Consumer banking has no such advantage.
C.ind: Mature; the story is self-help, not market growth.
C.risk: The restructuring stalling again - Citi has promised improved returns for fifteen years and not delivered.
C.implied: Below or near tangible book, the price implies returns stay structurally below peers. A re-rating needs execution, not a cycle.
C.debate: Bulls say a sum-of-parts discount closes as ROTCE improves toward the double digits. Bears say this is a value trap with a long track record.
C.disprove: ROTCE targets pushed out again; expense guidance missed; regulatory consent order penalties; transaction banking share loss.

SNDK.what: Sells NAND flash memory and storage products - the 2025 spin-off of SanDisk from Western Digital.
SNDK.rev: Client, consumer and cloud NAND storage. Data centre SSD demand is the growth swing factor.
SNDK.gm: Gross margin swings violently with NAND pricing, from negative in a glut to well above 30% in a shortage. There is no structural margin here.
SNDK.mgmt: David Goeckeler leads the separated company. Insider ownership small; the Kioxia joint venture governs fab capacity.
SNDK.comp: Samsung, SK Hynix/Solidigm, Micron, Kioxia (also its fab partner).
SNDK.moat: Scale and the Kioxia manufacturing joint venture. NAND is a commodity - the moat is thin and the cycle is the business.
SNDK.ind: NAND has been in an upcycle on AI storage demand after a brutal downturn.
SNDK.risk: The classic flash glut: capacity restarts meeting a demand pause, taking pricing down 30%+ in two quarters.
SNDK.implied: The price appears to extrapolate current cycle pricing. Check earnings against mid-cycle, not trailing.
SNDK.debate: Bulls say AI storage demand structurally lifts NAND. Bears say every flash upcycle since 2000 has ended in oversupply.
SNDK.disprove: NAND contract prices falling month over month; suppliers announcing capacity restarts; inventory days rising; hyperscaler SSD orders pushed out.

TMO.what: Sells laboratory instruments, reagents, consumables and contract research and manufacturing services to pharma, biotech and academia.
TMO.rev: Laboratory products and biopharma services ~45%, life sciences solutions ~15%, analytical instruments ~18%, speciality diagnostics ~12%. Pharma and biotech customers are over half.
TMO.gm: Gross margin around 41-43%. Consumables and reagents are high margin and recurring; instruments and services lower.
TMO.mgmt: Marc Casper has been CEO since 2009 with a strong record of accretive acquisitions. Insider ownership small.
TMO.comp: Danaher, Agilent, Sartorius, Merck KGaA, Lonza in bioprocessing and CDMO.
TMO.moat: Installed instruments that consume proprietary reagents, validated processes that regulators require you not to change, and unmatched catalogue breadth.
TMO.ind: Recovering from a post-pandemic destocking cycle plus weak China and biotech funding.
TMO.risk: Pharma R&D budget cuts from drug pricing pressure, plus China stimulus failing to revive instrument demand.
TMO.implied: A mid-20s P/E implies a return to mid single-digit organic growth after several flat years.
TMO.debate: Bulls call it the picks-and-shovels of biology with 80% recurring revenue. Bears note organic growth has been near zero for a while.
TMO.disprove: Organic growth not recovering above 4%; China revenue still declining; bioprocessing orders soft; pharma customers cutting R&D.

AXP.what: Issues premium charge and credit cards, lends to its cardholders, and runs its own payment network - it earns both the merchant fee and the interest.
AXP.rev: Discount revenue from merchants ~60%, net interest income ~25%, card fees ~15% and growing fast as annual fees rise. US around 70%.
AXP.gm: Watch net interest margin, the discount rate on billed business, and credit metrics. Premium customers default far less than the industry.
AXP.mgmt: Steve Squeri is CEO. Berkshire owns roughly 20% and has held it for decades - the single best endorsement in the S&P.
AXP.comp: Visa and Mastercard networks plus JPMorgan (Chase Sapphire) and Capital One in premium cards.
AXP.moat: A closed-loop network giving unique spend data, a premium brand that supports high annual fees, and an affluent customer base with structurally better credit.
AXP.ind: Premium card spend has grown faster than overall consumer spending, led by younger affluent customers.
AXP.risk: An affluent consumer recession hitting travel and dining billed business while card fee increases stop converting.
AXP.implied: A high-teens to low-20s P/E implies low-teens revenue growth and stable credit - reasonable if the premium consumer holds.
AXP.debate: Bulls say fee-paying premium members are the most durable consumer franchise in finance. Bears say it carries credit risk that Visa and Mastercard do not.
AXP.disprove: Net write-off rate rising above 2.5%; card fee growth slowing; billed business growth below GDP; Platinum refresh failing to retain members.

KLAC.what: Sells process control and inspection equipment - the tools that find defects on wafers - to every advanced chipmaker.
KLAC.rev: Semiconductor process control is the vast majority; services are roughly a quarter and recurring. Taiwan, Korea and China dominate the mix.
KLAC.gm: Gross margin around 61-63%, the highest in the equipment industry, because there is essentially no alternative supplier for the critical steps.
KLAC.mgmt: Rick Wallace has been CEO since 2006. Insider ownership small; capital return has been consistent.
KLAC.comp: Applied Materials and Onto Innovation in parts of inspection; in leading-edge process control KLA holds over half the market.
KLAC.moat: Near-monopoly share in optical inspection, an installed base under service contract, and the fact that yield tools pay for themselves - customers do not shop on price.
KLAC.ind: Process control intensity rises with each node and with advanced packaging - the best structural position in equipment.
KLAC.risk: China export controls removing a large revenue pocket, or a broad capex downturn.
KLAC.implied: A P/E in the 30s implies leading-edge capex intensity keeps rising and China does not fall away sharply.
KLAC.debate: Bulls say complexity means more inspection per wafer forever. Bears note the cyclicality and the China share of revenue.
KLAC.disprove: China revenue dropping below 20% without offsetting leading-edge orders; service growth slowing; foundry capex cuts.

CRM.what: Sells customer relationship management and enterprise applications - sales, service, marketing, analytics - by subscription.
CRM.rev: Sales Cloud, Service Cloud, Platform (including Slack), Marketing and Data Cloud. Subscription and support is over 90% of revenue. Americas ~65%.
CRM.gm: Gross margin around 77-78%. Mature SaaS economics; the debate is about growth, not margin.
CRM.mgmt: Co-founder Marc Benioff is CEO but owns only around 3%; activist investors pushed the shift from growth to profitability.
CRM.comp: Microsoft Dynamics, HubSpot, Adobe in marketing, SAP, ServiceNow and now AI-native application startups.
CRM.moat: Deep workflow embedding and data gravity - ripping out a CRM is a multi-year project - plus a large partner ecosystem.
CRM.ind: Application software growth has slowed; AI agents are both an opportunity and an existential question for seat-based pricing.
CRM.risk: AI agents reducing the number of seats enterprises need, which would break the pricing model that Salesforce is built on.
CRM.implied: A low-20s P/E on a software company implies the market has already priced slowing growth. The question is whether growth stabilises.
CRM.debate: Bulls say Agentforce monetises the installed base and the multiple is undemanding. Bears say seat-based software is the most AI-exposed business model in tech.
CRM.disprove: Current remaining performance obligation growth below 9%; Agentforce bookings not disclosed or disappointing; net retention falling; headcount-linked seat growth reversing.

VZ.what: Sells mobile and broadband connectivity to US consumers and businesses.
VZ.rev: Consumer roughly 75%, business ~25%. Wireless service revenue is the core; fixed wireless broadband is the growth line. Entirely US.
VZ.gm: Service margins are high but the business consumes enormous capital in spectrum and network - EBITDA margin near 35% matters more than gross margin.
VZ.mgmt: Dan Schulman took over as CEO in 2025. Insider ownership minimal; the dividend is the reason most people own it.
VZ.comp: AT&T, T-Mobile, cable companies (Comcast and Charter) reselling mobile.
VZ.moat: Spectrum licences, tower and fibre infrastructure, and regulatory barriers. Three-player market structure is the moat - but competition is intensifying.
VZ.ind: Mature and saturated; subscriber growth comes from switching, which costs promotional money.
VZ.risk: A price war triggered by cable operators taking mobile share, forcing the majors to compete on price.
VZ.implied: A single-digit P/E and a high dividend yield imply low growth and some risk of a payout problem - the market is not expecting much.
VZ.debate: Bulls say it is a bond-like yield with fibre and fixed wireless upside. Bears see a heavily indebted utility losing postpaid share.
VZ.disprove: Postpaid phone net losses; churn rising; dividend coverage from free cash flow deteriorating; net debt to EBITDA not falling.

AMGN.what: Sells biologic medicines in inflammation, oncology, bone health and rare disease, and is developing an obesity drug.
AMGN.rev: Repatha, Prolia/Evenity, Tezspire, Blincyto and the Horizon rare disease portfolio. US around 75%.
AMGN.gm: Gross margin around 65-70% reported. Biologics manufacturing is complex, which itself deters biosimilar competition.
AMGN.mgmt: Robert Bradway has been CEO since 2012. Insider ownership small; the Horizon acquisition added significant leverage.
AMGN.comp: AbbVie, J&J, Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly in obesity, plus biosimilar manufacturers attacking its older drugs.
AMGN.moat: Biologic manufacturing complexity, patents, and a rare disease portfolio with pricing power and few alternatives.
AMGN.ind: Mixed: legacy products face erosion, rare disease and inflammation are growing.
AMGN.risk: MariTide, the monthly obesity injectable, failing on tolerability - the pipeline value rests heavily on it.
AMGN.implied: A mid-teens P/E implies modest growth and some obesity option value, not a full success case.
AMGN.debate: Bulls get a dividend plus a free option on obesity. Bears note high debt from Horizon and biosimilar pressure on Prolia.
AMGN.disprove: MariTide phase 3 discontinuation rates staying high; Prolia erosion faster than expected; net debt not falling; Repatha growth slowing.

MRVL.what: Sells custom AI silicon, optical interconnect and networking chips to hyperscalers and telecom equipment makers.
MRVL.rev: Data centre is roughly three-quarters of revenue and rising; enterprise networking, carrier, consumer and auto the rest.
MRVL.gm: Gross margin around 50-60% depending on mix - custom ASICs carry lower margin than merchant optical products.
MRVL.mgmt: Matt Murphy is CEO. Insider ownership small; the company has been reshaped around AI infrastructure through acquisitions.
MRVL.comp: Broadcom above all in custom silicon, plus Astera Labs, Credo and in-house hyperscaler teams.
MRVL.moat: Electro-optics and SerDes IP leadership plus custom design wins that lock in multi-year programmes. Weaker than Broadcom on incumbency.
MRVL.ind: AI interconnect demand is growing very fast; the legacy segments are flat.
MRVL.risk: Losing an Amazon or Microsoft custom programme to Broadcom - a single socket loss is material.
MRVL.implied: The valuation implies custom silicon wins convert into large volume production revenue on schedule.
MRVL.debate: Bulls say optical and custom compute are the two fastest-growing AI budget lines. Bears point to concentration and Broadcom competition.
MRVL.disprove: A named custom programme delayed or lost; data centre revenue growth decelerating; gross margin falling as custom mix rises; guidance cuts.

TMUS.what: Sells mobile service and, increasingly, home broadband over 5G to US consumers and businesses.
TMUS.rev: Postpaid wireless service is the core, with fixed wireless broadband the growth line and prepaid (Metro) a large base. US only.
TMUS.gm: Service margins are strong; the Sprint merger synergies structurally lowered the cost base relative to peers.
TMUS.mgmt: Srini Gopalan succeeded Mike Sievert. Deutsche Telekom retains majority control, which shapes capital allocation.
TMUS.moat: The 2.5GHz mid-band spectrum position gives a genuine network cost and capacity advantage, plus scale post-Sprint.
TMUS.ind: Saturated market; T-Mobile has been the consistent share gainer.
TMUS.risk: Share gains ending as rivals match network quality, turning growth into a price war.
TMUS.implied: A low-20s P/E implies continued postpaid share gains and fixed wireless growth - a premium to the sector that requires outperformance to persist.
TMUS.debate: Bulls say the best network economics in US wireless with buyback capacity. Bears say the spectrum advantage is being closed and growth normalises.
TMUS.disprove: Postpaid phone net adds falling below peers; churn rising; fixed wireless additions slowing; promotional intensity rising across the industry.

APH.what: Sells connectors, cable assemblies and interconnect systems used in data centres, aircraft, vehicles and industrial equipment.
APH.rev: Communications solutions (including AI data centre) is the fastest-growing; harsh environment solutions (defence, industrial) and interconnect the rest. Truly global.
APH.gm: Gross margin around 33-35%. Thousands of engineered parts, each small in cost but critical in function - the classic high-return industrial niche.
APH.mgmt: Adam Norwitt has been CEO since 2009 and runs a highly decentralised acquisition machine. Insider ownership small.
APH.comp: TE Connectivity, Molex (Koch), Aptiv in automotive.
APH.moat: Designed-in components with qualification cycles, breadth across end markets, and a decentralised operating model that keeps acquisitions productive.
APH.ind: AI data centre interconnect demand has become a major growth driver on top of steady industrial markets.
APH.risk: An AI capex pause hitting the segment that has driven the re-rating, while industrial and auto remain soft.
APH.implied: A P/E in the high 30s implies AI-driven growth continues and the acquisition model keeps compounding.
APH.debate: Bulls say it is a quietly excellent compounder with 30 years of value-accretive deals. Bears say the multiple now embeds AI growth that was not there two years ago.
APH.disprove: IT datacom segment growth decelerating sharply; book-to-bill below 1; acquisition returns falling; industrial end markets not recovering.

QCOM.what: Sells smartphone system-on-chips and licenses its cellular patent portfolio - two very different businesses in one company.
QCOM.rev: QCT chips roughly 85% of revenue, QTL licensing ~15% of revenue but a large share of profit. Handsets ~75% of QCT; auto and IoT are the diversification.
QCOM.gm: Gross margin around 55-58%. Licensing is nearly pure profit; chips carry normal fabless economics.
QCOM.mgmt: Cristiano Amon is CEO. Insider ownership small; the strategy is diversifying away from Apple and handsets.
QCOM.comp: MediaTek in handsets, Apple in-house modems, Samsung LSI, NVIDIA and Mobileye in automotive compute.
QCOM.moat: An essential cellular patent portfolio that every handset maker must license, plus integration leadership in premium Android chips.
QCOM.ind: Handset units are flat; auto and edge AI are the growth vectors; the licensing base is stable but litigated.
QCOM.risk: Apple completing its in-house modem transition and Chinese OEMs shifting to MediaTek - both reduce QCT revenue directly.
QCOM.implied: A mid-teens P/E implies the Apple loss is manageable and auto and IoT fill the gap. The market is sceptical, which is why it is cheap.
QCOM.debate: Bulls see a cheap, cash-generative licensor with auto growth. Bears see the largest customer walking away on a known schedule.
QCOM.disprove: Apple modem shipping in volume; auto design-win pipeline not converting; licensing renewals on worse terms; Android premium share loss.
